extracted.intended_audience: general readers; students of law; journalists; persons researching tort/product-liability cases
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and factual/legal criteria relevant to assessing liability, damages, and corporate practices in a hot-coffee/product-liability lawsuit, using the Liebeck v. McDonald's case as a case study.

rubrics_metrics.name: Product defectiveness / unreasonably dangerous
rubrics_metrics.description: Liebeck's attorneys argued that, at 180–190 °F (82–88 °C), McDonald's coffee was defective, and more likely to cause serious injury than coffee served at any other establishment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to show the product (coffee as served) was 'unreasonably dangerous' and 'defectively manufactured'; supported by evidence of measured service temperatures and expert testimony about burn risk at those temperatures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparative negligence
rubrics_metrics.description: Applying the principles of comparative negligence, the jury found that McDonald's was 80% responsible for the incident and Liebeck was 20% at fault.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plaintiff's recovery is reduced proportionally by her share of fault (e.g., $200,000 compensatory reduced by 20% to $160,000). Comparative negligence is a key rubric for apportioning liability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adequacy of warning (warning sufficiency and prominence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Though there was a warning on the coffee cup, the jury decided it was neither large enough nor sufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluators consider not just existence of a warning but its size, prominence, and adequacy to inform users of the specific hazard; an inadequate warning may not shield a defendant from liability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior complaints and reports as notice of danger
rubrics_metrics.description: From 1982 to 1992, McDonald's had received more than 700 reports of people burned by its coffee to varying degrees of severity, and had settled claims arising from scalding injuries for more than $500,000.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A large number of prior incidents/settlements can demonstrate company's knowledge of the risk and support claims of negligence or punitive measures; used as evidence of notice and failure to act.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expert testimony on temperatures and burn times (causation evidence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Expert testimony that 190 °F (88 °C) coffee may produce third-degree burns in about three seconds and 180 °F (82 °C) coffee may produce such burns in about 12 to 15 seconds; lowering the temperature increases the time to injury.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scientific/medical expert evidence linking product condition (temperature) to injury severity and timing is used to establish causation and reasonableness of the product standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Company policy / operational standards (holding temperature requirement)
rubrics_metrics.description: McDonald's required franchisees to hold coffee at 180–190 °F (82–88 °C).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Internal corporate policies setting operating parameters can be used to show deliberate practices that create risk; such policies are weighed against safety obligations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risk–benefit justification (business reasons for hazardous practice)
rubrics_metrics.description: McDonald's claimed high initial temperature was to keep coffee hot for commuters and consultants advised that high temperatures are necessary in brewing to fully extract flavor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defendants may offer business-necessity or consumer-preference reasons for a practice; courts/juries weigh those claimed benefits against foreseeable risks and available safer alternatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Industry practice / comparative standard
rubrics_metrics.description: Attorneys presented evidence that coffee they had tested all over the city was served at a temperature at least 20 °F (11 °C) lower than McDonald's coffee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comparing defendant's practices to industry norms (other restaurants, trade associations) helps establish whether conduct deviates from reasonable standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Availability of safer alternatives / effectiveness of temperature reduction
rubrics_metrics.description: Lowering the temperature to 160 °F (71 °C) would increase the time for the coffee to produce such a burn to 20 seconds; these extra seconds could provide adequate time to remove the coffee from exposed skin.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrating practical, effective alternatives that materially reduce harm supports a finding that the original practice was unreasonable or defective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Severity of injuries and medical consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: The plaintiff suffered third-degree burns, was hospitalized for eight days while undergoing skin grafting, followed by two years of medical treatment, permanent disfigurement, and partial disability for two years.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The seriousness of physical injury, need for surgery/long-term care, and permanent effects are central to calculating compensatory damages and persuading factfinders of wrongful conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Settlements and pre-trial offers (negotiation posture)
rubrics_metrics.description: Liebeck sought to settle for $20,000; McDonald's offered $800; later offers/mediator suggestions (e.g., $225,000) were refused.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pre-trial settlement conduct and unreasonable refusal to settle can inform perceptions of culpability and may influence punitive damages or jury sympathy, though not determinative legally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Punitive damages: purpose and proportionality
rubrics_metrics.description: Jury awarded $2.7 million in punitive damages; the trial judge reduced punitive damages to three times the compensatory damages (totaling $640,000). Jurors used a revenue-based approach to arrive at the punitive figure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Punitive damages are intended to punish and deter; courts may review and reduce awards for proportionality. Calculation methods (e.g., multiples of compensatory damages or business revenue metrics) vary and are subject to judicial adjustment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gross negligence allegation
rubrics_metrics.description: The complaint accused McDonald's of gross negligence for selling coffee that was 'unreasonably dangerous' and 'defectively manufactured'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allegations of gross negligence (as opposed to ordinary negligence) can support higher punitive awards if the conduct is shown to be flagrant or reckless.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consumer behavior / empirical evidence about use
rubrics_metrics.description: It was found McDonald's had carried out research finding that customers intend to consume the coffee immediately while driving, undermining the commuter-keeping-warm justification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence about how consumers actually use the product (consumption timing, handling) bears on foreseeability of harm and reasonableness of safety measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remedial measures and publicity (post-incident response)
rubrics_metrics.description: McDonald's relied on more sternly worded warnings on cups to avoid future injury and liability and later statements about having lowered service temperature were disputed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Post-incident changes (warnings, design changes) are considered by courts, regulators, and public opinion; remedial action may mitigate risk but may not erase liability for past conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conflicting precedent across jurisdictions
rubrics_metrics.description: McMahon v. Bunn-O-Matic (Seventh Circuit) found 179 °F hot coffee was not 'unreasonably dangerous'; Bogle v. McDonald's (UK) rejected claim that serving at lower temperature would avoid injury.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different courts/jurisdictions can reach divergent conclusions on what constitutes 'unreasonably dangerous' — precedent influences but does not uniformly dictate outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of empirical comparative testing across establishments
rubrics_metrics.description: Attorneys presented testing showing other establishments' coffee served at substantially lower temperatures than McDonald's.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Systematic empirical comparisons are persuasive to show deviation from common practice and to quantify the extent of excess risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Calculating compensatory damages (actual and anticipated expenses)
rubrics_metrics.description: Liebeck's past medical expenses were $10,500; anticipated future medical expenses approximately $2,500; daughter's loss of income approx. $5,000; jury awarded $200,000 in compensatory damages (later reduced by plaintiff's fault).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compensatory damages aim to cover actual past and reasonably foreseeable future medical costs, lost income, and non-economic losses; calculations may reflect both documented costs and broader harm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public/media framing and its influence on tort-reform debates
rubrics_metrics.description: The Liebeck case became a flashpoint in the debate over tort reform and was widely portrayed as an example of frivolous litigation; others argued media portrayals misrepresented the facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While not a legal standard, media framing affects public understanding, legislative debate, and the broader policy context around tort awards and reform proposals.
